statement: Clothes have become so cheap that many people now buy new items frequently and throw them away after wearing them only a few times.
question: What problems does this cause? What solutions can you suggest?
model:
A T-shirt can now cost less than a sandwich, and for many shoppers clothing has become almost disposable. This culture of so-called fast fashion causes serious environmental and social harm, but a combination of regulation and changing consumer habits could reduce its impact considerably.

The most obvious problem is the sheer volume of waste. Millions of tonnes of garments are discarded every year, and because most are made from synthetic fibres such as polyester, they can take centuries to decompose in landfill. Much of the clothing donated to charity in wealthy countries is shipped abroad, and in places like Ghana, unwanted bales now pile up on beaches and riverbanks. Production itself is also damaging: growing cotton requires vast quantities of water, while dyeing fabric pollutes rivers in manufacturing regions with toxic chemicals. Furthermore, the relentless pressure to produce cheaply contributes to low wages and unsafe conditions in factories, as the collapse of the Rana Plaza building in Bangladesh in 2013 tragically demonstrated.

Tackling these problems requires action at several levels. Governments could make manufacturers financially responsible for collecting and recycling the clothes they sell, a policy France has already begun to introduce. This would give companies an incentive to design garments that last longer and can be easily recycled. Tax relief on repair services, as introduced in Sweden, would also make mending a jacket cheaper than replacing it.

Consumers have a role to play as well. Buying fewer, better-made items, using second-hand shops and online resale platforms, and swapping clothes with friends can all extend the life of each garment. Schools could revive basic sewing skills, which have largely disappeared in many countries.

In conclusion, the throwaway approach to clothing places a heavy burden on the environment and on garment workers. However, by making producers accountable and encouraging a culture of repair and reuse, its damage can be significantly reduced.
